en: Letter to a Disciple.
Om. Homage to the Triple Gem.

Even today, because of his songs concerning the extremely difficult deeds of his former lives, which are sung by the beautiful women of the gods and *kiṃnaras*, the forest-like clusters of lotus-faces of Māra’s maidens shrink away as if at the rays of the moon. (1)

He whose body was charming with good fortune, who was most excellent, whose sight was difficult for those of little merit to obtain, and who fulfilled the desires of people according to their wishes—his sole activity was the essence of altruism, like a wish-fulfilling gem. (2)
He who was always of a single flavor with the sole happiness of others, through the suffering of others experienced supreme suffering;
for him, whose quality of great compassion was exceedingly established, his own suffering and pleasure were entirely eclipsed. (3)

For him whose head became a lotus for the sake of others when he offered it as a gift, the earth became a white parasol for his own sake; yet [for those who oppose him], it was like the sharpened edge of a sword. 4.

By him, who delights in benefiting the world, whose rising is manifest, who possesses the strength of pure virtues, and who shatters the darkness of faults—by him, as by the delightful moon that has arisen, the world was illuminated. (5)

His auspicious teaching, which possesses unbroken and pure conduct like a supreme jewel worn as a crest-ornament upon the great hoods of serpents, wipes away the darkness of dissolution at the very summit of the netherworld.
Like a cloud of Dharma arisen for the benefit of others, he rained down the water of the nectar of Dharma with a single flavor;
yet, because of the suffering of the world, that [nectar] took on many flavors.
In vessels that have wide, deep, stainless, and clearly manifest bases, and which are capable of enduring all friction, whatever is placed within them becomes beneficial to all people. (8)

Those who do not attain, drink, or uphold that vigilance which removes death, birth, and old age, are afflicted by the great intoxication of abundant delusion and are scorched by the heat of worldly existence. 9.

That they abandon delusion after attaining that eye which is the single, stainless one for the entire world, the common property of all, and the sole lamp of the three realms—that is the supreme wonder of one who has been utterly struck by fortune. (10)

Placing their steps upon the rungs of the stairway to the palace of enlightenment, which consists of the stages of training, they proceed toward the lofty path without turning back; yet when they turn back, they descend to their own original ground. ||11||
Who in this world, desiring to cross the ocean of birth which is so difficult to traverse, would cast away the raft of ethical conduct already within their grasp?
How could one fallen into the midst of a wilderness, having encountered a noble caravan, not grieve for a long time, being ignorant of the good path? (12)

Those who, striving to rise from the abyss within the cave of the mountain of saṃsāra and from the supreme darkness, cast away the offering of the Jina’s virtues along the way, fall swiftly with a violent descent into the depths below. (13)

Even when alone, those who, having mentally established a discipline, uplift themselves through the accumulation of action—they are the virtuous ones who have become the crowns of the world's circle; by them alone do true teachers attain their status as gurus through their excellent disciples.

Those resplendent ones, who are devoted to abiding in truth and follow her whose heart is inwardly pure—she who, like a mother, gives birth to a flood of virtues—happily renounce even their lives, but never their promise. (15)
Let alone all the slanders of the people here, and all the miserable states of sin and the terrible hells;
for that this noble person immediately abandons his innate nature—what other suffering on earth could there be greater than that? (16)

He who, having reached the vast vessel made of Dharma that has been well-prepared by the sages, yet abandons its path once more—his mind is made restless by desire amidst the dancing of the revolutions of the ocean of saṃsāra, despite his observance of rules. (17)

He who, mounting the wheel of saṃsāra that revolves incessantly, imagines he is attaining happiness while it is turning, will inevitably, driven by the power of karma, gradually pass through all the high and low states of existence. (18)

Having entered the womb-abode, which is obstructed by a mass of extremely foul-smelling impurities, utterly cramped, and filled with dense darkness—just like a hell—he endures great suffering with his limbs huddled together. (19)
In the course of time, he then somehow reaches the earth as if being crushed by a heavy oil-press;
yet, even so, that very fact that he does not immediately abandon his life is due to the difficulty of attaining a state where such suffering can be experienced.

Remaining there in that impurity, revolving within it with his body enveloped by the moist *kalala* and *arbuda*, and emitting a great and pungent odor, he—being tormented as if by loathing—abandons that [womb] like a burst ulcer of a former memory when its morbid humors have reached a violent state of suppuration. (21)

Having abandoned childhood—rendered helpless by all its trappings and characterized by limbs that were slack and agitated—the state of non-existence (death) arises; then, within the high mountain-caves of youth, which are the abodes of the poison of the objects of the senses, one is deluded.
From that state as well, he falls down unconscious; yet even when fallen, he does not abandon his agitation.
Thus the fool continues to regard his own body as something charming, free from old age and death.
Abandoning the excellent path frequented by the lords of sages, he wanders on a wrong track, deluded;
like an elephant in rut, unrestrained and crushing everything in his path with impetuous force. (24)
Then, as if an elephant-driver were acting upon an elephant, Old Age—placing her feet mercilessly upon his head against his will—forcibly applies the sharp goad of grey hair. ||25||
Even though his conduct was thus crooked, he performed virtuous deeds out of fear and other motives; deluded, he acted like a flowering arrow for the sake of his own destruction. (26)
Then Antaka, as if laughing, proceeds to swallow him from the head with floods of grey hair like terrifying fangs— the disease of old age, whose pacification is impossible.
Then his joints fall apart, his intellect departs, and his capacity for movement fails;
his body wastes away, yet the hope for life inevitably increases. (28)

And gradually, with his senses closed and his power destroyed, though still longing for sense-objects, he reaches that state which awaits him in hell; if it exists at all, it is truly terrifying. (29)
"How was this done by me? How was it not done thus? My course is ruined!
How was it that I did not notice this snake as its foot was placed upon my head? (30)
Thus his mind was afflicted by mental agonies born of evil deeds and filled with grief;
he was looked upon with compassion by his kinsmen, who were themselves diseased with tears.
With its vital organs and joints crushed, as if entering a most terrible darkness, it abandons its own dear body, which was protected with great effort. (32)
With his hair seized and bound by firm nooses, he wails, held fast by the messengers of Yama;
yet people do not hear his speech, being distracted by the clamor of their own cries of lamentation. (33)

On paths difficult to traverse due to sprawling mountains, rivers, and dense thickets of exceedingly sharp thorns, he—his neck already gripped by the noose of Time—is dragged along by the terrible agents of Death wielding the staff of Yama. (34)
When one who is intensely thirsty sees pure water from afar, he approaches it with the desire to drink;
yet that very same water becomes a source of distress when it is fouled by a mire of putrid pus mixed with a mass of hair and moss. (35)
The Malaya mountain, with its peaks cooled by spray tossed by the breezes of the evening and its dark sandalwood trees, retreats;
yet even it becomes jagged with heaps of extinguished firebrands licked and shattered by the fierce flames of a forest conflagration. (36)
Even that ocean, which possesses a mass of foam intensified by the breaking of fierce and tossing waves as it approaches, becomes like a parched, white,
and dreadful sandy bank through the wind of his arrow.

As he stands there, foreboding the arrival of the clouds, the bearer of water pours down upon his body a shower of iron arrows—consisting of sparks from charcoal, smoke, thunderbolts, and stones—reddened by the streak of lightning like a line of molten gold. (38)
To one afflicted by heat, even a beneficial breeze feels like fire; to one afflicted by cold, even fire provides coolness.
To one deluded by the ripening of extremely fierce karma, this entire universe then appears as its very opposite. (39)
As Śūcīmukha, whose belly is fearsome for many yojanas, drinks water from the great ocean in his distress,

even before the drops reach his broad throat-cavity, they are completely dried up by the heat of the phlegm. His body is pulverized, wounded by the thunderbolt-like tips of the fangs of the snarling, thick-bodied dogs.
On the banks of the Vaitaraṇī river, which is filled with caustic water, one is dragged across jagged rocks sharpened to the edge of a blade. ||41||

Running with speed, his body severed upon beds of sharpened razors and in forests of sword-blade creepers, he falls helpless into a well—the mouth of Death, conquered by sharp spears, pikes, darts, swords, and maces. (42)
With his body emaciated by the intense heat and exhausted by unbearable suffering, he approaches the trees with their thick, dark green leaves;
yet, his form pierced by hundreds of falling leaf-weapons, he remains there for a long time, crying out, with his cries as his only companion. (43)
He is embraced by women who, with their jeweled bracelets blazing amidst garlands of sparks from hundreds of flames issuing from their extremities, are as cruel as a saw in their merciless passion.
With his entire body crushed and shattered by the impact with herds of goats as terrifying and formidable as mountains,
and his life-breath snuffed out by the chill of a gust of wind, he is likewise ground to powder again and again by the hundreds.
Terrified by thousands of *sukharakhaḍgas* and *śivās*, he mounts that *kūṭaśālmali* tree once more with rapid strides,
his body pierced by a mass of downward-pointing thorns that inflict deep wounds.

For one who is firmly bound by the coils of Time, which are like venomous serpents with raised hoods as if fallen from the hand of Death, the cranes, crows, herons, and vultures forcibly pluck out the quivering eyes while he remains there. (47)

With their mouths resembling the points of thunderbolts, they forcibly tear at his body as he lies asleep; crying out in agony, his form pierced by many iron-tipped, sharp spikes, he descends, deprived of consciousness. (48)

There, some with their bodies pierced by flaming spears and sharp arrows were unable to descend; while others, their entrails and sinews torn apart as they were dragged by fierce, sharpened iron weapons with razor-like points, were torn asunder. (49)

Some fall upon the rugged slopes of mountains; some enter the interior of oil-pans that have been heated until they sizzle; others, unable to find a place to set foot, enter a ground of glowing sand strewn with flying sparks. (50)
Furthermore, some whose young and putrid bodies are shattered by swarms of tiny, wriggling insects, unable to move even so much as a twitch, live on, their lives bound by the noose of karma. (51)
Even their bones, being carried away by a cold that was beyond comparison, caused their limbs to become shattered, trembling, and shriveled;
they were covered with hundreds of erupting and bursting boils, and from the wounds bitten by swarms of insects, marrow, fat, and streams of lymph flowed out. ||52||

With their teeth clenched together and their hair and body-hair standing on end, with their eyes, ears, and throats pierced by the piercing cold, these beings—possessing bodies that have reached a state of extreme mental dullness—remain in the cold hells, wailing intensely. (53)

The atmosphere was turned smoky-grey by scattered, abundant, and fierce-smelling pungent smoke; the circle of the quarters was made formidable by the mass of the hands of its spreading flames; adorned with heaps of white bones and skeletons, the terrifying Bhairava appeared as if he had arrived, brandishing his sword and skin and uttering cries of "Hā! Hā! (54).
In some places, filled with sparks from leaping trees making the sound *caṭacchaḍhat*, and in others, where the expansion [of the fire] is momentarily obscured by fat making the sound *chamacchamad*;
in the hollows of the chest, amidst unstable darkness, there fall the fires of hell, sounding *kaṭatkadad*, which have surpassed the fire at the end of an aeon.

With ribs burning from the decayed old straw, their bodies like withered creepers emitting sudden flashes of flame, they are terrified by the entrails gushing out from their bursting bellies; their only remaining activity is the emission of deep, rattling groans. (56)
Having repeatedly observed a gap in the cave that was opened from afar, those seeking refuge from the suffering of delusion somehow proceed toward it;
yet when even that is blocked by the firm hands of karma, their desires rendered fruitless, they go instead to some other state of misery. (57)

Following the incessant rain of blazing, sharp javelins, those struck by the fierce staffs of hell drink molten iron that is ablaze with garlands of fiery rays; their mouths, ears, and nostrils spew forth smoke as they swallow it while their fluids flow out.

With the mass of his tawny flames ignited by the brains from their skulls and eyes, which were scorched and split open, he becomes as merciless toward the heaps of their bodies as a fire upon a pile of dry fuel. (59)
Those living beings whose lives are as unstable as the waters of mountain torrents find that very same parching heat in the hells, and those same fires;
indeed, their own actions transform everything in such a way that it appears utterly dreadful.

For a living being who has somehow escaped from hell—the abode of evil—after being helplessly and painfully entangled by his own karma, human birth is indeed extremely difficult to obtain in worlds agitated by the fear of infinite varieties of rebirths. (61)

Or if he should take birth among the Mlecchas who observe vows equal to those of the hell-wardens, or among animals that devour one another— by indulging in such very same conduct, he falls once again into the abyss.

Having attained that which enables one to cross even the ocean of birth, which plants the seed of supreme awakening in Śiva, and which surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem in its abundance of virtues—who here would render this human state fruitless? (63)
Having attained this human state, which is exceedingly difficult to find, one should accomplish that very thing which is desired.
For there is no certainty of stability for even a single moment in this life, which is as flickering as the flame of a lamp tossed by a violent wind. (64)

While people are thinking, "This task must be done tomorrow," or "This other one today," or "This one after a mere moment" or "This one right now," I suspect that the impatient and enraged Kṛtānta (the God of Death) laughs, his staff of Time stained orange by his sidelong glances.

"The *phullṛ* flower has arrived; this is the onset of spring; the moon-blossomed autumn has come"—at these thoughts people rejoice, yet I do not; rather, my life is ebbing away, and thus I fall into extreme despondency. (66)

In the mountain peaks and forest glades where the moon’s orb serves as a near and swelling ornament, and which are girdled by heavy clouds resting upon them—glades that are free from worldly attachment—the fortunate spend their lives, whose nature is as flickering as the wind. (67)

Is that delight found in the grounds of the Nandana grove, upon the stone slabs of the hips of celestial damsels—which are frequented by throngs of most charming celestial maidens and are lovely, auspicious, and free from attachment—that which is found in the forest regions? (68)

Did she find such delight in the celestial rivers with their pure waters and secluded, lovely banks—where the fragrance of divine women has vanished and which spread the laughter of blooming *saṃtānaka* blossoms—as she did in the forest streams? (69)

The vast caves of the mountains—delightful because they are free from the bustle of people, possessing deep expanses, and encircled by streaks of green forest—are situated near riverbanks; yet, being inaccessible even to the gods due to the sweet fragrance of the celestial *suraja* flowers, they seem to say to travelers: "This is the fire of worldly suffering. (70)
Desires and worldly possessions, as well as women, have been declared by the Jina to be like illusions, mirages, the moon reflected in water, and waves;
yet fools, deceived by the delusions that are as fleeting as those found within a dream, fall even into those hells where beings exist. (71)
Sense objects are like poison, sweet only for a fleeting moment; sense objects are like poison, bitter in their ultimate consequence.
Sense objects are like poison, a dense thicket of the darkness of delusion; sense objects are like poison, as turbulent and swift as an irresistible torrent. (72)
Desires and sense-objects are like poison; when considered carefully, poison is better than sense-objects, for their nature is inherently poisonous.
Poison remains poisonous within a single lifetime, whereas sense-objects turn into poison even in future births. (73)
Poison and sense-objects have an exceedingly difficult range;
poison kills when consumed, but sense-objects kill even from mere remembrance.
Poison mixed with poison attains pacification when treated by those who hold antidotes and possess effective mantras;
or, when properly administered, poison may even be for the benefit of men. But the great poison of the sense-objects is never like this.

Just as a deer, standing on the edge of a treacherous pit overgrown with sprouts of durvā grass and longing for them with its mind, falls into the abyss—and yet that very fall is its gain—so too is this world of living beings, whose minds are possessed by pleasure. (76)

Having enjoyed playful excursions with the Apsarases, their tresses disheveled by the currents of the Mandākinī, they wander once more upon the harsh Vaitaraṇī, enduring terrible suffering shattered by contact with its waves. (77)

Having sported in the divine groves with their beloveds upon couches spread with the leaves of the Kalpavṛkṣa trees after performing sacrifices, they wander once more through the regions of the Sword-Leaf Forest (Asipattravana), their limbs mangled by the falling of sharp and agitated weapons. (78)
Having wandered for a long time upon the slopes of Mount Meru, where the footfalls are alternately raised and lowered with pleasant sensations to the touch,
they roam about with their feet and thighs scorched by a mass of fire consisting of heated sand and hot ashes.
Having gone to heaven in celestial chariots bristling with clusters of necklaces and garlands of tinkling, radiant kiṅkiṇīs,
they fall again headlong into the terrible, stable, immeasurable, and shoreless darkness of the nether regions.

Even Śakra, whose footstool is made tawny by the mass of light from the crests of gods, kiṃnaras, nāgas, and yakṣas, goes to a miserable state when driven by the wind of his own karma; what man indeed would not feel fear in such a place? (81)

With their hair disheveled and their bodies smeared with dust, wearing only soiled garments, and having consecrated their circle of kinsmen to the vow of compassion, even the gods undergo supreme suffering at the time of death; yet humans—whose lives are as flickering as bubbles on water—do not [suffer] in such a way. (82)
In this world, which is terrifying due to the cessation of the intense flames of suffering, people maintain the conceit that they are happy;
yet that is the gaping, wide-open mouth of Death, and the very seed of the tree of rebirth once again. (83)

Bound by the firm and long threads consisting of craving, with the terrifying staff of Time cast down and aimed at it, this is like a fishhook set by Death for sentient beings who are floundering in the ocean of existence. (84)

Having emerged from the intense heat of the boiling, thick mire of the Kumbhīpāka hell, and having obtained a moment's release through breaths of relief, the denizens of hell—being struck by many iron mallets filled with fury—regard that very [beating] as supreme happiness, just as it is. (85)

Thus, being incessantly and helplessly tormented by those dreadful sufferings for such a long time, and having somehow escaped the agitation of the hells and old age, when his own unbearable boat of suffering has momentarily become calm, the world, alas, develops a thirst for the mere attainment of a small measure of physical pleasure. (86)
As long as the notion of happiness arises anywhere in the entire world, so long does the fire of passion arise with increasingly fierce flames;
as long as the cultivation of virtue continues to spread, so long does the darkness of delusion grow ever more dense.
To the extent that the cultivation of the foul reaches increase, to that same extent the darkness of delusion becomes more and more tremulous. (88)

When poets compare the lotus, the jasmine, and the blue water-lily to the limbs of women—though those limbs are foul-smelling, putrid, and deformed—the terrible fruit of that falsehood is this: they themselves enter into the womb within those very women.
What destination in this world has one not traversed hundreds of times? What pleasure has one not experienced many times before?
What riches, with their charming smiles like flickering whisks, have one not obtained? And yet, attachment continues to increase. (90)

There are no rivers that have not been crossed by them, nor are there sandy banks upon which they have not left their tracks; there is no place in this world where they have not made their dwelling, nor is there any spot in the sky where they have not traveled. Yet, despite all this, their insatiable passion only continues to increase. (91)
There is no suffering that has not been experienced repeatedly in the past; there are no sensual pleasures in this world through which one has not found satisfaction;
and there is no sentient being who has not lain within a womb—nevertheless, how is it that detachment does not arise? (92)

In this vast world, as one undergoes birth and repeatedly wanders through many cycles of suffering and happiness, there is no person in this world who has not been a kinsman; yet even so, the serpent of hatred remains with its terrifying coils. (93)

With whom I have come together to laugh, to sport, to sing, and to drink and eat in one place; with whom I have held conversations and spent many delightful years; and with whom I have somehow traversed various conditions, both pleasant and painful, as time passed—[where are they now? (94)

Beholding them—lost amidst the whirlpools as they were swallowed by the jaws of the turning waves of the ocean of worldly existence—if one abandons these kinsmen and departs alone, then there is no such thing as an ungrateful person. (95)

Who indeed—even a bandit—would venture to abandon those women whose breast-milk was drunk with affection by helpless infants held upon their laps, and who were the sole recipients of such abundant and unrestrained fondling? 96.

Who indeed—even an enemy—would venture to depart here, having abandoned those who, though confined within the womb, made room for him; who, with minds softened by the flow of affection, bore him aloft with ease; and who are now suffering, helpless, and miserable? (97)

In this world scattered by floods of suffering, helpless and without refuge, noble beings consider that very pain which they endure for the sake of others to be true happiness. Even compared to those who, for a mere moment, find relief from hunger, thirst, heat, and fatigue by drinking the water of a mirage, who here could possibly be their equal? (98)

Neither by armies nor by the trappings of royal fortune, nor by wives, nor by children, nor by dwelling in the abode of the gods, nor by going to the realm of the asuras, can those devoted to sensual enjoyment ever obtain that joy which those dedicated to establishing the welfare and happiness of others attain—joy that is somehow accessible even within the pleasures of the sensory world. (99)
Even a beast eats fodder that is easily obtained on its own, or drinks water when it is parched with thirst, having found it by chance;
but if this man here exerts himself to accomplish the welfare of another, that is his true splendor—this indeed is happiness, and this is true manliness! 100.
That the sun wanders about creating light with its tireless horses, and that the earth, bearing an incalculable burden, maintains constant light—this is no personal interest of theirs;
rather, it is simply the nature of the great that they find their sole delight in the essence of the welfare and happiness of the world. (101)

Beholding the world fallen helplessly into the blazing fire of suffering, enveloped by the confused and agitated course of the blinding smoke of ignorance—those men who here quickly proceed toward it, appearing like a head-wrap scorched by the flickering flames of a forest fire, are the truly virtuous. (102)

Though it is filled with the flames of fire, they plunge into the Avīci hell; though their hair stands on end and it is as cool as a mass of snow or moonbeams, this lotus pond—though its blooming lotuses smile like laughter—causes them torment as if it were a conflagration of fire. 103.
The virtuous, having girded their loins for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, dwell happily even in the Forest of Sword-leaves;
they do not, however, take delight for even a moment in the Nandana grove, accompanied by the beauties of the gods.
Having themselves crossed over, these steadfast ones cross the Vaitaraṇī river once again for the sake of ferrying across those people who have no refuge;
yet they do not themselves indulge in the pleasure of contact with the shifting play of the waves of the celestial river.

Thus, worship Him—the limit of good conduct, the ornament of ornaments, the auspicious nectar, the noble among the radiant, difficult for the ungrateful to attain, the delight of those who rejoice, the cause of equal happiness for all, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things. (106)
The flower of the Sugata’s word should always be cultivated; like the flowers of trees, it bears a magnificent fruit.
From the flower of the Sugata’s word, a mass of meaning is extracted by those who desire its excellence, just as honey is gathered from flowers by bees. (107)
Abandon the objects of the senses, which are crowded with worldly affairs and perish in an instant; pursue that equanimity which is free from longing yet attended by the fear of Death.
Dispel the darkness of delusion and remove the bolt of hypocrisy; for noble stallions do not indeed sleep for very long. 108.
With the Vinaya as its spreading branches, the aggregate of vigor as its trunk, patience as its level roots, tranquility as its flowers, wisdom as its limbs, and generosity as its thick foliage;

with aspiration as its peak, ethical conduct as its shade, and bestowing the fruit of perfect peace—you, O Lord, be the one great tree for those afflicted by the heat in the desert of worldly existence! 109.
O you who are beneficial to many, do not fear; let there be the great roar of your speech, a vast torrent of pure streams impelled by the wind of compassion.
Having stilled the dust and adorned the earth with the shade of your virtue, become the one great cloud for those suffering from the heat in the desert of worldly existence. 110.
Manifestly vast, with bottomless mud, providing a most delightful refuge, perpetually cool, and free from the danger of lurking serpents;
naturally beautiful, cutting off thirst and protecting against the weight of oppression—be you the one great lake for those afflicted by the heat in this desert! 111.

Whatever merit has been acquired by me through this *Tigada* [The Sharp Sword] concerning the life of the Sugata, may all people, having cultivated faith therein, be constantly happy, possessing delightful enjoyments, with their wishes fulfilled, and delighting in the welfare of others, thereby gradually attain omniscience. (112)

May the hells possess abundant splendor, their surfaces as level as the palms of hands, clearly illuminated, with their fires extinguished; covered by the leaves of land-lotuses, bristling with lotus shoots, pure and fragrant, their grounds adorned with blooming lotuses, and cooled by breezes laden with spray. (113)

May the desired births of the Buddhas occur in every direction at all times—births that shatter the hosts of Māra with their triumphant cries, proclaim the sound of fearlessness, delight men and gods in the playful sport of the waters of the sky, and destroy the continuous succession of birth, death, affliction, and exhaustion. (114)
May there be for the worlds the fragrance of Dharma, a great festival of literary compositions; may the desires of Death remain barren for a long time;
and may the auspicious light of the moon, perpetually cooled by the continuous rains of assemblies for the discourse of sages and Janakas, attain its fulfillment. 115.
Thus ends the religious poem titled *Śiṣyalekha*.
The work of the master Ācārya Candragomin.
